activityGoals.name: Creating a List of Words from a File
activityGoals.goalDescription: Construct a program that reads a text file and creates a list of the words that the file contains, ignoring the case of the letters. Assume that all of the words in the text file are separated by a single space characters.
activityGoals.correctOutput: words = [the, wheels, on, the, bus, go, round, and, round]

lineList.content: //Step 1: Define the method that creates a list of words from a file

commentList: We need to declare the method that creates an ArrayList of words that the given file contains. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as ArrayList of String, as it returns an ArrayList that holds String values.

lineList.content: //Step 1.1: Create an empty list to store the words

commentList: We need to have a list that could store String values because each word is a String. The following statement creates an empty ArrayList for storing Strings and assigns its reference to variable words. We use ArrayList instead of an array because arrays have fixed length while ArrayList is dynamic in size. In situations like this that we don't know the maximum number of elements that we have to process, we need to use ArrayList. As elements are added to an ArrayList its capacity grows automatically.

lineList.content: //Step 1.2.1: Wrap a BufferedReader around a FileReader

commentList: We want to read a text file; therefore, we need to use a FileReader and wrap it in a BufferedReader. This statement create a FileReader object using the new keyword and empty parentheses. The variable fr holds a reference to a FileReader object.
We wrap a BufferedReader around the FileReader because the BufferedReader buffers the input to make the reading process much faster. The variable br holds a reference to a BufferedReader object.

lineList.content: //Step 1.2.2: Use the BufferedReader object to read one line at a time

commentList: We define a string variable to hold the content of each line that the BufferedReader object reads from the file. We set it to null.

We need to read the lines as long as we have not reached the end of the file. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the line that is read is not null.

We could read a line by invoking the readLine method of the BufferedReader object. Here, we compare the result of calling the readLine method to null. We assign the result of calling the readLine method to variable line because we need to process it in the body of the while loop.
The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the line that is read is not null. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to false, that is when the line that is read is null.

lineList.content: //Split the line into words, ignoring the case of the letters

commentList: We need to split the line into words and store the words in an array. We don’t care about capitalization, so we convert the line to lowecase before splitting it into words.

We convert the string characters into lowercase by calling the method toLowerCase on that string. We use split() method with " " as its argument because we want the split method to separate strings using a single space character.

lineList.content: //Add each word in the line to the list

commentList: We use a for loop to iterate over the words and add each word to the ArrayList. We can do this by using for–each statement that visits each word in the array of line tokens. This for loop assigns the name token to each of the values in the array in turn, from left to right, and then the statement in the loop body will be executed for each value.
This method adds the word that we visited to the end of the list.
We can add an element to the ArrayList by calling the add() method.

activityGoals.name: Comparing the List of Words from Two Files
activityGoals.goalDescription: Construct a program that reads two text files and creates a list of the words that each of these files contains, ignoring the case of the letters. The program should determine which list is larger in size, i.e., which list has more words.\nAssume that all of the words in these text files are separated by a single space characters.
activityGoals.correctOutput:
list1 words = [the, wheels, on, the, bus, go, round, and, round]
list2 words = [the, wipers, on, the, bus, go, swish, swish]
list1 has more words.

public void compareLists(ArrayList<String> list1, ArrayList<String> list2 ) {
commentList: We need to declare the method that compares two lists to find the one that is larger in size. The first parameter is the reference to the first list, and the second parameter is the reference to the second list. Both parameters have the type ArrayList of String because both lists store String values. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as void, as it does not return any values.

To determine the list that is larger in size, we need to perform two tests: one for determining whether the first list has more elements that the second list, and one for determining whether the second list has more elements that the first list. If the none of the lists has more elements than the other, then we could conclude that both lists have the same size.
We can determine the number of elements of an ArrayList by calling the size() method.

The conditions that test which list has more elements are mutually exclusive (i.e., one and only one of the conditions can be true); therefore, their order does not matter. Also, it is better to use if-else if statements instead of sequential if statements because only one test could be true and once we find which list is larger than the other, we don't need to perform more tests.
If the first list has more elements than the second list, then the body of this if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this if statement is skipped.
This statement prints that the first list has more words. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
If the first test fails (i.e., when the first list is not larger than the second list), we need to test if the second list has more elements than the first list.

If the first test fails (i.e., when the first list is not larger than the second list), the body of the previous if statement will not be executed, instead the program jumps to this else if statement where we test whether the second list has more elements than the first list.

If the second list has more elements than the first list, then the body of this else if statement gets executed. Otherwise, the body of this else if statement is skipped.
This statement prints that the second list has more words. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
We need to end the above if-else if statements with an else statement that its body is executed when none of the above tests are true, that is when both of the lists have the same size.
Note than when we end series of if-else if statements with an else statement, we make sure to execute the body of exactly one of those statements.
